subjects.name: Civics (American Government, History, Symbols and Holidays)

chapters.name: Principles of American Government
chapters.summary: The form of government, the Constitution and its amendments, the Bill of Rights, the Declaration of Independence, the rule of law, and why power is split into three branches (official questions 1-15).
keyPoints: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land, and it has 27 amendments.
The first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights.
Power is split into three branches so one part does not become too powerful (checks and balances).

chapters.name: Congress (Legislative Branch)
chapters.summary: The three branches, the two parts of Congress, the number and terms of senators and representatives, who they represent, and who elects them (official questions 16-35).
keyPoints: Congress (the legislative branch) writes laws and has two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
There are 100 senators (two from each state) who serve six-year terms.
There are 435 voting members of the House, who serve two-year terms.

chapters.name: The President and the Executive Branch
chapters.summary: The President's term and term limit, who takes over if the President cannot serve, the powers of the President, the Cabinet, and the Electoral College (official questions 36-49).
keyPoints: The President is elected for four years and can serve only two terms.
If the President can no longer serve, the Vice President becomes President.
The President is Commander in Chief of the military, signs bills into law, and vetoes bills.

chapters.name: The Courts and Federal and State Powers
chapters.summary: The judicial branch and the Supreme Court, how long justices serve, and the powers that belong only to the federal government or only to the states (official questions 50-62).
keyPoints: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States.
Supreme Court justices serve for life, so they can be independent of politics.
Printing paper money and declaring war are federal powers; providing schooling and giving driver's licenses are state powers.

chapters.name: Rights and Responsibilities
chapters.summary: Voting amendments, who can vote and serve on a jury, rights of everyone living in the U.S., the Pledge of Allegiance, the Oath of Allegiance, and ways to serve the country (official questions 63-72).
keyPoints: Only U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury.
Everyone living in the U.S. has rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of religion.
Men age 18 through 25 must register for the Selective Service.

chapters.name: Colonial Period and Independence
chapters.summary: Why colonists came, American Indians, slavery, the Revolutionary War, the Declaration of Independence, the original 13 states, the Constitution of 1787, the Federalist Papers, and the founders (official questions 73-89).
keyPoints: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, adopted on July 4, 1776.
The Constitution was written in 1787 at the Constitutional Convention.
James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, and John Jay wrote the Federalist Papers.

chapters.name: The 1800s
chapters.summary: The Louisiana Purchase, wars of the 1800s, the Civil War, Abraham Lincoln, the Emancipation Proclamation, the amendments after the Civil War, and the women's rights movement (official questions 90-99).
keyPoints: The United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803.
The Civil War was the war between the North and the South, and it ended slavery.
The Emancipation Proclamation freed the slaves in the Confederacy (Confederate states).

chapters.name: Recent American History
chapters.summary: Wars of the 1900s, women's right to vote, the Great Depression, World War II, the Cold War, the civil rights movement, September 11, 2001, and American innovations (official questions 100-118).
keyPoints: Franklin Roosevelt was President during the Great Depression and World War II.
The United States entered World War II because Japan attacked Pearl Harbor.
Martin Luther King, Jr. fought for civil rights and equality for all Americans.

chapters.name: Symbols and Holidays
chapters.summary: The capital, the Statue of Liberty, the flag's stripes and stars, the national anthem, the motto E Pluribus Unum, and national holidays (official questions 119-128).
keyPoints: The flag has 13 stripes for the 13 original colonies and 50 stars for the 50 states.
The national anthem is The Star-Spangled Banner.
Independence Day celebrates the country's independence from Great Britain.
